rationale: The federal OSHA-covered employer uses a hazardous chemical and is introducing a new chemical hazard in employees' work area without prior hazard training. It must provide effective training, including the specified hazard, detection, protective-measure, labeling-program, and SDS content; maintain an SDS; maintain a written hazard communication program; and ensure decanted workplace containers are labeled unless the immediate-use portable-container exception applies. The supplied facts do not establish that exception, so the general workplace-container labeling obligation applies.

The technician's newly assigned role triggers Hazard Communication information and training at initial assignment for hazardous chemicals in the work area. The training must cover detection methods, relevant chemical hazards, protective measures, and the employer's hazard communication program details. The supplied facts do not establish an impending introduction of highly hazardous chemicals or a new/modified facility startup, so the pre-startup safety-review requirement is not selected.

Because federal OSHA PSM applies and the equipment and technology modification is not a replacement in kind, the employer must manage the change through written management-of-change procedures. The modification changes process safety information, so that information must be updated, and operating procedures must be reviewed and updated to reflect the changed equipment and technology. Before highly hazardous chemicals are introduced and production restarts, a pre-startup safety review must verify design conformance, adequate procedures, completed management of change for the modified facility, and completed operator training.

Because Federal OSHA PSM applies and this incident at a covered process could reasonably have resulted in a catastrophic toxic release, the employer must investigate the incident. No employee injury occurred, so the supplied injury, fatality, and hospitalization reporting or recordkeeping requirements are not triggered by the stated facts.

Because the federally regulated establishment is required to keep Part 1904 records and had 300 employees during the covered year, it must create and certify its OSHA 300A annual summary, post it conspicuously without alteration, defacement, or coverage, electronically submit 300A information annually, and retain the specified Part 1904 records for five years following the covered calendar year.

The approaching anniversary of the last review triggers the annual periodic-inspection requirement for the machine-specific energy-control procedure. The employer must conduct the inspection at least annually to verify that the procedure and the standard's requirements are followed.

The scenario expressly states that this is covered servicing under the federal hazardous-energy-control standard and identifies a risk of unexpected startup and stored pneumatic-energy release causing injury. The employer therefore needs an energy-control program and documented energy-control procedures. Before employees enter the machine, required energy-isolating devices must isolate the machine from its energy sources, and stored or residual pneumatic energy must be relieved, disconnected, restrained, or otherwise rendered safe.

Federal OSHA PSM is stated to apply, and the contractor will enter a covered process area with known fire, explosion, and toxic-release hazards. Because the contractor is being selected, the employer must obtain and evaluate its safety performance and programs. The employer must inform the contract employer of the relevant known hazards and control contractor entrance, presence, and exit through safe work practices. The contract employer must ensure each contract employee is instructed in job- and process-related hazards and applicable emergency-action-plan provisions. The employer also must maintain the required contract-employee injury and illness log for contractor work in process areas. Hot-work, management-of-change, and HazCom requirements are not selected because the scenario does not establish their factual predicates.

The requester is a former employee seeking the OSHA 301 Incident Report describing their own injury. The employer maintains the requested report and is covered by federal OSHA recordkeeping rules. The employer must provide a copy containing that information by the end of the next business day.

The request is from an authorized employee representative and concerns OSHA 301 Incident Reports for represented employees at an establishment. The employer must provide copies within seven calendar days, limited to the OSHA 301 section titled "Tell us about the case," with all other information removed.

The fatality arose from a work-related incident at a recordkeeping-covered establishment and is a new case. Death satisfies the general recording criteria, so the case must be recorded. The employer also must report the fatality to OSHA within eight hours after the death.

The work-related amputation and in-patient hospitalization trigger OSHA reporting within 24 hours. The case is stated to be recordable, so it must be entered on the OSHA 300 Log and OSHA 301 Incident Report within seven calendar days after the employer received the information.

The employee orientation supports applicability of the duty to inform each employee of the injury/illness reporting procedure. The supervisor's threat of discipline following the employee's report is conduct that may deter or discourage accurate reporting and is inconsistent with the prohibition on discharging or otherwise discriminating against an employee for reporting a work-related injury or illness. No facts establish that the injury is recordable or reportable to OSHA, so incident-recording and severe-incident reporting requirements are not selected.

The process is stated to be covered by federal OSHA PSM, and the three-year compliance audit has identified deficiencies requiring corrective action. The employer must promptly determine and document an appropriate response to each audit finding and document correction of the deficiencies.

The scheduled inspection of covered-process equipment implicates the inspection and documentation requirement. Because the vessel was found outside acceptable limits, the employer must correct the deficiency before further use, unless necessary measures can assure safe operation while correction is completed safely and timely.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: A qualified engineering/safety determination is needed to establish the acceptable limits, whether the vessel may remain in operation under necessary safe-operation measures, and the appropriate corrective action and timing.

rationale: Federal OSHA Hazard Communication applies, the employer uses the hazardous chemical in the employee's work area, and the employee could not immediately access its safety data sheet during a work shift. The employer must ensure safety data sheets are readily accessible during each work shift to employees in their work areas; electronic or alternative access may not create barriers to immediate access.

The portable container was filled from a labeled drum, is intended only for the immediate use of the employee who performed the transfer, remains under that employee's control, and is not stored for later use. Therefore, the portable-container immediate-use labeling exception applies; the employer is not required to label this portable container.

The lock must ordinarily be removed by the employee who applied it. Because that employee is unavailable, another employee may remove it only under employer direction using documented specific procedures and training that provide equivalent safety. The scenario does not establish that such a documented procedure exists, that it covers this removal, or that the person directed to remove the lock has received the required training.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: Confirm whether the employer has documented, specific off-site-employee lock-removal procedures that provide equivalent safety and whether the proposed remover is trained and acting under employer direction. Without those facts, removal by another employee cannot be determined compliant.

rationale: Because hazardous chemicals of one employer may expose another employer's workers at a shared worksite, the employer's written hazard communication program must specify methods for providing the other employer on-site SDS access and for communicating precautionary measures and the labeling system. A written hazard communication program is also required at each workplace.

The reactor is in a federal OSHA PSM-covered process, and the proposed component swap is an equipment change. The replacement-in-kind exception applies only if the component is technically equivalent. The maintenance records identify a different material specification and operating limit, while engineering and operations disagree about equivalence. This conflict requires qualified engineering and process-safety judgment to determine whether the exception applies or whether management-of-change procedures are required.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: Obtain and resolve a documented technical equivalency determination comparing the existing and proposed component design/material specifications, operating limits, and impacts on the covered process. If it is not a replacement in kind, apply the written management-of-change procedure before implementation.

rationale: For a federal-OSHA-covered establishment, OSHA notification within 24 hours is required only when the employee's in-patient hospitalization resulted from a work-related incident. The supplied facts establish neither work-relatedness nor that the hospital admission was an in-patient hospitalization.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: Determine whether the illness resulted from a work-related incident and whether the hospital admission was for in-patient treatment. If both are true, report the event to OSHA within 24 hours.

rationale: Federal OSHA hazard communication training is required when a new chemical hazard about which employees have not previously been trained is introduced into their work area. The supplied facts establish procurement of a new cleaning product, but do not establish that it is hazardous or that it presents a hazard not already covered by employees' prior training.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: Obtain the product safety data sheet or other hazard classification information and compare its identified hazards with the hazards covered by affected employees' existing training records.

rationale: Outside vendor maintenance triggers the need to assess whether the work is covered by the lockout/tagout standard. If unexpected energization, startup, or release of stored energy could occur and cause injury, the equipment must be isolated under the energy-control program, and the site employer and outside employer must inform each other of their respective lockout/tagout procedures.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: Determine whether the vendor's maintenance exposes workers to potential injury from unexpected energization, startup, or release of stored or residual energy. Without that fact, it cannot be determined whether the maintenance is covered and therefore whether the outside-personnel coordination requirement applies.

rationale: The establishment's 75 employees places it in the 20-249 employee range, and it keeps Part 1904 records. Electronic annual submission of Form 300A information applies to establishments in that size range only if they are classified in an industry listed in Appendix A to Subpart E of 29 CFR Part 1904. The industry classification is not supplied.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: Provide the establishment's industry classification (NAICS) or confirmation whether it is listed in Appendix A to Subpart E of 29 CFR Part 1904.
